### Iran’s Nuclear Red Line: Could Tehran Trigger a New U.S.-Israel Strike?

Could renewed Iranian nuclear activity trigger another military confrontation with Israel and the United States?  
 In this TV7 Israel News Update, Jonathan Hessen is joined by Brig. Gen. (Res.) Yossi Kuperwasser and Col. (Ret.) Joel Rayburn to examine Iran’s nuclear strategy, the pressure surrounding the Strait of Hormuz, and Tehran’s use of regional proxies to threaten vital energy routes and infrastructure.  
 The discussion also looks at the Houthi threat in the Red Sea, growing regional military coordination, pressure on Saudi Arabia, Iraqi militias, Hezbollah’s position in Lebanon, and the continuing pressure on Hamas in Gaza.

# US officials met Iran-aligned Houthis in Oman - Reuters

Iran-aligned Houthi fighters pose next to a captured vehicle following what the source described as an attack on Saudi-backed forces in the location given by the source as al Jawf governorate, Yemen, in this screengrab taken from a video released by Houthi Military Media on September 15, 2026



US officials met representatives of Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis in Oman over the weekend, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing five sources familiar with the matter, days after the group seized a strategic stretch of Yemen's Red Sea coast.

The previously undisclosed meeting was held at the US Embassy in Muscat, three of the sources told Reuters. Two said Oman, a longtime regional mediator, helped organize the talks.

One source said the meeting took place on Sunday. US embassy personnel represented Washington, while the Houthi delegation included senior official Mohammad Abdulsalam, who is under US sanctions, and Abdelmalik al-Ajiri, according to Reuters.

**Houthis say US ships not a target**

The Houthis told US officials they did not intend to attack American vessels and remained committed to a ceasefire reached with Washington in 2025, two sources told Reuters.

A Yemeni source said the group also said it would not attack Israeli ships or other commercial vessels, except those belonging to Saudi Arabia.

# No rush for peace: Why a broad peace in Ukraine remains elusive

In the absence of conditions for a broad agreement, upcoming meeting between Zelenskyy and Trump during UN General Assembly could offer next opportunity to test prospects for limited truce

Maksym Skrypchenko

16 September 2026•Update: 16 September 2026

Archive

![Content media](https://web-cdnprod.aa.com.tr/uploads/Contents/2026/09/16/thumbs_b_c_348a5c9fb2ce1d70708e68c036add339.jpg)

ISTANBUL

* Maksym Skrypchenko is the president of the Transatlantic Dialogue Center, a Ukrainian think tank.

Recent trips to Moscow and Kyiv by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, preceded by a visit by CIA Director John Ratcliffe, marked a new attempt by Washington to jumpstart negotiations on ending the Russia-Ukraine war. However, the intensity of diplomatic contacts currently far outweighs their tangible results. The reason lies not so much in the lack of an acceptable peace formula as in the fundamentally different expectations the parties hold concerning the war's continuation: Ukraine seeks ways to stop the destruction, while Russia hopes that, in the coming months, Kyiv will no longer be able to keep resisting.

Russia has recently [ramped up its attacks](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/9/11/us-diplomacy-under-fire-as-moscow-escalates-attacks-on-ukrainian-officials) on Ukraine, further fuelling some fears in the West that Ukraine could end up [losing the war](https://spectator.com/article/ukraine-is-losing-the-war-kushner-witkoff/).

Tellingly, however, the main thrust of discussions led by the Russian president had a different focus: fuel, trade and transit.
